sites.name: 1905 Mine
sites.location: Hurricane Hill / Boulder County Tungsten Mining District
overview: The 1905 Mine was a small but documented tungsten producer beside Hurricane Hill Road in the Boulder County tungsten district.
USGS records place the mine 825 feet south 25 degrees west of the Vasco No. 1 shaft and describe shaft workings associated with a ferberite-bearing vein along the Hurricane Hill breccia reef.

timeline.text: USGS indicates the mine may have produced tungsten before the surviving detailed production records begin.
The mine was productive during the World War I tungsten boom. Incomplete USGS records document about 250 units of WO3 from ore averaging 12.9 percent WO3.
USGS reported no known later production and estimated that total historic output may have exceeded 1,000 units of WO3.

moreHistory: U.S. Geological Survey Professional Paper 245 describes the 1905 Mine at roughly 8,550 feet elevation beside Hurricane Hill Road. The documented position is relative to the Vasco No. 1 shaft, which provides a defensible historic mine-level Scan anchor while avoiding a claim that the exact shaft collar has been surveyed by Remnant.

The mine was developed by shaft workings that USGS believed were probably no more than about 150 feet deep. The vein lies in the hanging wall of the Hurricane Hill breccia reef, striking roughly northeast and dipping northwest through aplite and granite.

USGS attributes the property to Gold, Silver, & Tungsten, Inc. during the documented production period. The retained production figures are incomplete, so Remnant presents them as reported historical estimates rather than precise lifetime totals.

sites.name: Afterthought Mine
overview: The Afterthought Mine is a documented Jamestown Mining District fluorspar locality west of Jamestown with a stable mapped mine/tunnel anchor.
Federal mineral records preserve the site as a fluorite occurrence and modern USGS-derived mapping places the mine at approximately 40.12221, -105.40055.

timeline.text: The Afterthought workings were developed as part of the Jamestown district's fluorspar and metal-mining landscape.
Federal Jamestown-district mineral mapping retained the Afterthought Mine as a named fluorite locality.
USGS/GNIS-derived mapping preserves a stable mine-level point for identification, though Remnant does not claim that point is a field-surveyed portal collar.

moreHistory: USGS-linked mineral references identify the Afterthought Mine in Boulder County's Jamestown Mining District and record fluorite at the locality.

The mapped Afterthought Mine and Walker Tunnel share the same published mine-level coordinate, so Remnant treats the coordinate as a defensible locality anchor rather than asserting a specific surviving opening without field confirmation.
No defensible site-specific photograph with clear app-use rights was found in the media search; unrelated Jamestown mine photographs were rejected rather than attached to the wrong location.

sites.name: Acme Mine
overview: The Acme Mine was a major Louisville-area coal mine that operated from the late nineteenth century into 1928 and helped shape the town's industrial landscape.
Historic state and local records document deep shaft workings, company housing, railroad service, and repeated subsidence effects beneath Louisville.

timeline.text: The Acme Mine entered operation in Louisville during the expansion of Boulder County's northern coal field.
Colorado's coal-mine inspector described the Acme as a two-shaft mine about 190 feet deep, connected to the Colorado & Southern Railroad.
Rocky Mountain Fuel Company acquired the Acme and operated it through its final years.
Industrial Commission records document 81 Acme employees in a wage case involving Rocky Mountain Fuel Company.
The Acme Mine closed after decades of coal production beneath and around Louisville.

moreHistory: Colorado mine-inspector records describe a main shaft and air shaft serving a roughly six-foot coal seam, with the main shaft divided for hoisting, pipe lines, and emergency access.
Local historical records preserve 1911 photographs of the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company's Acme Mine and company houses, confirming the mine's substantial surface plant and community setting.
Historic Louisville research also documents subsidence associated with Acme workings beneath the town, showing how the mine's underground footprint affected the later urban landscape.

For Remnant identification, the USGS/GNIS mine point at approximately 39.98193, -105.13665 is used as the documented mine-level anchor rather than claiming a surviving shaft collar has been field-surveyed.

sites.name: Ajax Mine
overview: Ajax Mine is a documented inactive coal mine in Boulder County's Louisville-area coal field. Boulder County historical material retains the Ajax name in the Harney-Lastoka mining landscape, while mapped place data provides a stable mine-level location for identification.

timeline.text: Boulder County's retained Harney-Lastoka historical research identifies the Ajax coal mine as established in 1890.
The mine formed part of the Louisville-area coal landscape that shaped local settlement and employment.

moreHistory: A mapped mine point at approximately 39.977763, -105.136652 is retained as a defensible historic mine-level Scan anchor. Remnant does not represent that point as a field-surveyed surviving shaft collar.
A focused media search did not locate a reusable exact-site Ajax photograph; similarly named Ajax mines elsewhere in Colorado were rejected as wrong-site material.

sites.name: Albion Mine
sites.location: Lake Albion / Snowy Range Mining District
overview: Albion Mine is a documented historic mine locality near Lake Albion in Boulder County's Snowy Range Mining District.

Historic Boulder County sources place Camp Albion at the center of the Snowy Range district, while retained mineral-locality mapping provides a defensible mine-level identification point for Albion without claiming that a surviving opening has been field-surveyed.

timeline.text: The Snowy Range Mining District was organized during Boulder County's early mining period; later sources also called it the Albion Mining District after the nearby camp.
A Denver Public Library mining-place index records the Albion Mine as established by 1864.
Camp Albion developed as a small mining center near timberline and became the focal settlement of the Snowy Range district.

moreHistory: Boulder historical collections describe Camp Albion as a small western Boulder County mining center associated with the Snowy Range Mining District and preserve photographs of the camp and its ore-milling landscape.

A mapped Albion mineral locality at approximately 40.05000, -105.58528 is retained as the Basic Scan anchor. Remnant treats this as a defensible historic mine-level locality point, not as a claim that an open shaft, adit, or exact surviving collar has been field-verified.

Known archival Camp Albion photographs document the surrounding mining settlement rather than the exact Albion Mine component, and their item-level reuse terms do not provide a sufficiently clear basis for packaging them as the mine's app image.
